1. Start here

This lecture is easiest when you refuse to memorize “pulmonary hypertension” as one disease. First confirm elevated pulmonary pressure, then ask where the pressure is coming from, then classify the clinical group, then connect the mechanism to the RV.

Must know
mPAP >20→Check wedge→Pre vs post-capillary→Assign Group 1–5→Treat the mechanism
>20 mmHg
mPAP defines PH

This is the lecturer’s #1 takeaway. Older ≥25 mmHg definitions are outdated for this course.

RHC definitive
Echo screens, cath confirms

RHC gives mPAP, wedge, CO and PVR—the data needed to classify the hemodynamic phenotype.

Syncope high risk
Dyspnea is common; syncope is dangerous

Syncope means cardiac-output reserve is failing and was taught as functional class IV.

Repeatable question-solving approach

1. Is PH present?→2. Wedge high or normal?→3. Which clinical group?→4. What is happening to PVR / RV / CO?→5. Which treatment logic fits?

Reverse reasoning: If the stem starts with JVD, RV heave, D-shaped LV, syncope, or a low cardiac index, work backward to chronic RV pressure overload and then ask what raised PVR or left-sided filling pressure.

5. Recognition lab

Train the patterns you are likely to be shown: hemodynamics, ECG, CXR, echo, pathology and cath waveforms.

Hemodynamic sorter

Pick a case, classify it before revealing the answer.

Pathology recognition

Ask: What wall layers are thickened and why does the lumen matter?

Medial hypertrophy + intimal hyperplasia. This is structural remodeling of small pulmonary arteries/arterioles, narrowing the lumen and increasing PVR.

ECG recognition

Look for: rightward forces and strain.

Lecture clues: right axis deviation, RVH, RV strain with T-wave inversion/ST depression in V1–V3, and peaked P waves in lead II from RA enlargement.

CXR recognition

Look for: central vs distal pulmonary vessels.

Dilated central pulmonary arteries with distal arterial attenuation/pruning and right-sided cardiac enlargement. Suggestive but not definitive.

Echo: pressure overload

Ask: What chamber is pressurized enough to distort the septum?

RV pressure overload flattens the septum → D-shaped LV. Severe RV dilation can also compress left-sided filling.

Cath waveform clue

Ask: How do you distinguish RV from PA?

Pulmonary artery: dicrotic notch + higher diastolic pressure. RV: large systolic upstroke but low diastolic pressure and no pulmonic-valve closure notch.

Integrated final review. It is intentionally longer than one page so the lecture does not get compressed into a misleading one-liner list.

Part I — Core framework & must-know content

Core map: Pulmonary vascular/left-heart/lung/clot trigger → ↑mPAP → use wedge to localize source → use PVR + clinical context to classify group → chronic RV afterload → RV hypertrophy/dilation → ↓CO → syncope/RHF.

Definitions you should be able to write from memory

TermLecture-ready definition
PHmPAP >20 mmHg at rest by right-heart catheterization.
Pre-capillary PHmPAP >20 + PAWP ≤15; in PAH, PVR >2 WU.
Post-capillary PHmPAP >20 + PAWP >15 → pressure transmitted from left heart.
PAHGroup 1 pulmonary arteriolar vasculopathy with precapillary hemodynamics after excluding other precapillary causes.

The one equation the slide expects you to interpret

RVSP = 4v² + RAP

v = tricuspid-regurgitant jet velocity; RAP = estimated right atrial pressure. In the absence of pulmonic stenosis, RVSP approximates PASP. Interpretation: faster TR jet → much higher estimated RV/PAs pressure because velocity is squared.

Supplemental clarification: PVR = (mPAP − PAWP) / CO. Use it conceptually: higher transpulmonary pressure gradient or lower CO → higher resistance.

Group 1 pathogenesis: memorize the direction, understand the why

↓ NO / ↓ prostacyclin+↑ endothelin→vasoconstriction + proliferation→medial hypertrophy / intimal fibrosis / plexiform lesions→↑PVR→RV failure
PAH subtype / associationLecture anchorTrap
Idiopathic PAHNo clear cause after extensive workup; lecture states ~½ of PAHDo not call it “PPH”; that term is outdated.
Heritable PAHBMPR2 emphasizedSame Group 1 hemodynamics/pathology, different etiology.
CTD-associatedScleroderma/systemic sclerosis is the key associationScleroderma can also cause Group 3 ILD or Group 2 disease.
Congenital shuntChronic shear stress; larger/higher-pressure lesions carry greater riskNot all congenital heart disease patients have PAH.
PortopulmonaryPortal hypertension must be presentDo not equate cirrhosis alone with PAH without portal HTN.
HIV-associatedRecognized Group 1 associationDyspnea still needs full differential/classification.
Drug/toxin-associatedMethamphetamine heavily emphasized; fenfluramine/cocaine also discussedMethotrexate was the “least likely” answer.

Presentation & examination

Most common presentation

Progressive exertional dyspnea. Also fatigue, chest discomfort, palpitations, dizziness/lightheadedness.

Hypoxia is not the most common presenting symptom; significant PAH may exist with near-normal resting oxygen saturation.

Most concerning symptom

Syncope → inability to augment CO → cerebral hypoperfusion. Lecturer: automatically functional class IV.

Right-heart-failure clues: JVD, edema, ascites, RV S3; plus RV heave, loud P2, TR murmur, Graham Steell murmur.

Functional class: translate activity into severity

ClassLecture wordingExam interpretation
INo symptoms with ordinary physical activityFunctionally well despite diagnosis
IISymptoms with ordinary activity; slight limitationMild limitation
IIISymptoms with less than ordinary activity; marked limitationRoutine activities provoke symptoms
IVSymptoms with any activity or at rest; syncopeSevere/high-risk; lecturer moves syncope here

Progression: do not be fooled by a falling PA pressure

PhasePVRPA pressureCOMeaning
Compensated↑↑PreservedRV still generating pressure
Symptomatic/decompensating↑↑HighStarts fallingSymptoms emerge
Late decompensatedSeverely ↑May fallLowRV cannot generate forward flow/pressure

Treatment logic

Strategy/pathwayWhy it helpsExamples from slideCourse nuance
Endothelin receptor antagonismBlocks excess vasoconstrictor/proliferative endothelin signalingBosentan, macitentan, ambrisentanKnow pathway & class first
NO–cGMP pathwayAugments vasodilator signalingSildenafil, tadalafil, riociguatRiociguat also appears in Group 4 treatment context on slide
Prostacyclin/IP pathwayReplaces/augments deficient vasodilator and antiproliferative signalingEpoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost, selexipagParenteral therapy is emphasized for high-risk disease
Activin signaling inhibitionTargets disease biology/remodelingSotaterceptNewest pathway highlighted
CCB in vasoreactive respondersWorks only in the small acute-responder phenotypeCalcium-channel blockersNot routine empiric therapy
General measuresReduce RV congestion, correct hypoxemia, preserve functionDiuretics, oxygen when needed, rehab/exercise, vaccinationsAnticoagulation no longer routine for all PAH
NuanceGeneral measures from the transcript: patients should be euvolemic (not overloaded, not over-diuresed); oxygen is for hypoxemia; stable patients should exercise as tolerated; pregnancy is treated as very high risk; high altitude can worsen symptoms through hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

Professor-style “yes/no” rules

YES: All PAH etiologies can share similar vasculopathic findings, including plexiform lesions.
NO: Lung biopsy is not routinely required; severe PH patients may tolerate invasive cardiopulmonary procedures poorly.
YES: Exercise is encouraged when stable and symptom-limited.
NO: Hypoxia is not the most common presenting symptom.
YES: CTEPH may have a surgical treatment option.
NO: Anticoagulation is not automatically given to every modern PAH patient just because small-vessel thrombosis can appear histologically.

Lower-priority but testable treatment goals from slide 72

Low-risk features shown in the lecture include WHO FC I–II, 6-minute walk distance >440 m, BNP <50 ng/L or NT-proBNP <300 ng/L, preserved/improved RV function, RAP <8 mmHg, CI ≥2.5 L/min/m², SvO₂ >65%, and no progression/syncope/RHF hospitalization. The lecturer’s bigger message: reassess repeatedly and escalate until low-risk status is achieved/maintained.

Clarification 1 — wedge threshold

The slide text writes PAH wedge pressure “<15 mmHg,” while the transcript says “15 or less.” Current ESC/ERS hemodynamic criteria use PAWP ≤15 mmHg for precapillary PH. For course reasoning, treat 15 as the upper boundary of a non-elevated wedge.

Clarification 2 — PVR unit mismatch on slide 8

The slide pairs PVR >2 WU with 240 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Those values are not numerically equivalent: 240 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ corresponds to the older 3-WU threshold. The current definition uses PVR >2 WU. The guide therefore prioritizes the WU threshold taught in the lecture and current guideline.

Clarification 3 — sleep-disordered breathing

The lecture groups sleep-disordered breathing/hypoventilation under Group 3. Modern ESC/ERS guidance more specifically emphasizes hypoventilation syndromes and notes that isolated nocturnal OSA alone is generally not a direct PH cause. For this course, preserve the lecturer’s broader framework unless a question explicitly asks current guideline nuance.

Lecture priority

The lecturer repeatedly emphasized that you should know the definition, five groups, Group 1 vasculopathy, RHC diagnosis, symptoms, and treatment pathways. Individual drug names were shown for completeness but were explicitly de-emphasized.

External clarification source: 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension, European Heart Journal 43(38):3618–3731. This Learning Lab does not require internet access to function; the guideline is only used to reconcile the threshold discrepancies above.
